title.script: Welcome to the Class Fifteen capstone workshop. Today is different from a normal lecture: the important voices in the live room will be yours, and the final evidence will leave with you as a portfolio story. I am Mira, an AI teaching assistant. This is a synthetic voice. Leo and Xiaoyu, when you hear them, are simulated classmates rather than real students. This recording prepares your deck, timing, defense, online portfolio project card, and resume link. It does not replace the live showcase, your own research presentation, or the instructor's questions. No real student's name, project, data, or result appears here. The running Palmer Penguins example is a computed classroom demonstration from public ecological teaching data; it is not student work and it does not claim universal performance. Your goal is not to sound certain about everything. Your goal is to make one supported conclusion easy to inspect, answer questions with honest boundaries, and give a future reviewer a safe route back to the evidence.

A stronger-sounding sentence is not a stronger result.

reflection-story.script: Reflection makes intellectual growth visible. Use three moves: I first assumed, the evidence showed, so I revised. A strong reflection names a concrete decision, the evidence that challenged it, and the claim, method, or next question that changed. A weak reflection says I learned a lot about AI, but gives the reviewer no trace of what changed. Specific revision is evidence of research maturity. A null result or failed approach can support an excellent reflection because it shows how the evidence constrained your belief rather than merely decorating it.
